questions.question: Explain what non-conventional energy sources are, the two properties that define them, and the evidence that South Africa is exceptionally endowed, including the programme that delivers the build.
questions.expected_answer: Non-conventional sources are the alternatives to the established fossil-and-nuclear order — solar and wind above all, plus biomass and biogas, geothermal, wave and tidal power, and small hydro; most are renewable, replenishing naturally. Two properties define them: the fuel is free — sunshine and wind arrive without mining, railing or importing, so nearly all cost lies in building the harvesting equipment, paid once and productive for decades — and the flows are intermittent, since the sun sets and the wind drops, so supply must be paired with storage, backup or a designed mix. South Africa's endowment is world-class: most of the interior receives more than 2 500 sunshine hours per year, with the Northern Cape among the premium solar territories on earth, while two oceans drive strong, usable wind onto the Eastern, Western and Northern Cape coasts; Germany built a world-leading solar industry with roughly half our sunshine, proving the constraint was never the resource. Delivery runs through the REIPPPP — the Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme — under which private developers bid competitively to build wind and solar farms and sell power on long contracts; since 2011 it has drawn hundreds of billions of rand and built over a hundred plants, with auctions driving prices below the cost of new coal per kilowatt-hour.

questions.question: Compare photovoltaic and concentrated solar power, and describe wind energy generation, giving South African and world examples of each technology.
questions.expected_answer: Photovoltaic panels convert sunlight directly into electricity in semiconductor cells — no moving parts, no water, no noise — with output following daylight instantly, peaking at noon and vanishing at dusk; they scale from rooftops, which boomed during load-shedding, to the mega-farms around Upington and De Aar, and solar water heaters remain the cheapest solar of all. Concentrated solar power instead uses fields of tracking mirrors to focus heat onto a receiver where molten salt is heated to hundreds of degrees; the heat raises steam and drives a conventional turbine, and because hot salt stores cheaply in insulated tanks, CSP generates for hours after sunset — Khi Solar One near Upington, KaXu and Xina at Pofadder, and Redstone near Postmasburg with twelve hours of storage built to serve the evening peak. Wind turbines convert moving air to electricity through aerodynamic blades turning a generator; power rises with swept area and the cube of wind speed — double the wind, eight times the power — so towers exceed a hundred metres. South Africa's wind belt is coastal: Jeffreys Bay and Cookhouse in the leading Eastern Cape, Caledon and Darling in the Western Cape, with turbines sharing veld with grazing sheep and paying land rentals and community revenue shares. World examples: China dominates manufacturing and installed capacity in both technologies; Germany proved policy beats cloud; Morocco's Noor complex is Africa's CSP giant; Denmark generates roughly half its electricity from wind; and the North Sea nations lead offshore wind.

questions.question: Evaluate the future of non-conventional energy in South Africa: its effects on the economy and the environment, the obstacles that will decide its pace, and a concluding judgement.
questions.expected_answer: Economic effects: new wind and solar are now the cheapest new power available, restraining future tariffs; REIPPPP has attracted hundreds of billions of rand in private investment; construction and maintenance jobs, land rentals and community trust revenues flow to rural provinces such as the Northern Cape that industry previously passed by; and localisation offers a green manufacturing ladder. Against this, coal employs on the order of ninety thousand miners concentrated in Mpumalanga towns with few alternatives, and renewables employ fewer permanent workers, mostly in other provinces — so the transition redistributes work, which is why a just transition matters: retraining, pensions, new industry located in coal country, and international climate finance to fund it. Environmental effects are overwhelmingly positive against the coal baseline — no carbon dioxide, no sulphur dioxide smog, and almost no water use in a dry country — though honest accounting notes land footprints, bird and bat mortality without careful siting, and the material demands of manufacturing and disposing of panels, blades and batteries. The obstacles deciding pace: the grid, since the best resources lie in the Northern and Eastern Cape far from Gauteng's demand and transmission lines are full — now the binding constraint; intermittency, managed by the mix of storage, CSP, pumped storage and complementary wind; and policy certainty, since investment follows reliable auction rounds. Conclusion: the future is not a question of resource — South Africa's is world-class — but of delivery; sun and wind will take a growing share, and only the speed is in dispute.
